questions.question: You are editing an integration's conf.yaml. Which characters may you use to indent nested keys in YAML?
choices: Spaces only, never tab characters
Tabs only, never space characters
Tabs or spaces, if a file uses only one kind
Any whitespace; YAML ignores indentation
questions.explanation: The YAML specification states that tab characters must not be used in indentation because different systems treat tabs differently, so nesting is expressed with spaces. Using tabs consistently throughout a file does not make them legal, and indentation is significant in YAML because it decides which keys belong to which parent.

questions.question:
Both of these datadog.yaml fragments set host tags:

tags: ["env:prod", "team:web"]

tags:
  - "env:prod"
  - "team:web"

How does the Agent interpret them?
choices: Only the dashed form is a valid YAML list
The bracketed form is one tag with a comma
Both define the same list containing two tags
The dashed form creates a map with two keys
questions.explanation: YAML sequences can be written in flow style (square brackets, comma-separated) or block style (one '- ' entry per line), and Datadog's tagging docs call the two forms functionally equivalent. The bracketed form is a real list rather than a single string, and dashes mark list entries, not mapping keys.

questions.question:
A fresh datadog.yaml contains:

## @param logs_enabled - boolean - optional - default: false
## @env DD_LOGS_ENABLED - boolean - optional - default: false
#
# logs_enabled: false

Which edit turns on log collection?
choices: Change default: false to default: true in the ## @param line
Delete the two ## lines so the Agent falls back to true
Add logs_enabled: true indented two spaces under the # line
Replace the last line with logs_enabled: true at column 0
questions.explanation: Lines beginning with # are YAML comments, so the ## @param and ## @env lines are documentation only and editing or deleting them changes nothing. You enable the feature by uncommenting the setting and setting it to true as an unindented top-level key; the documented default is false. Indenting the key would misalign it with the other top-level keys.

questions.question:
The datadog.yaml example contains these lines (documentation comments omitted):

# process_config:
#   process_collection:
#     enabled: false

An engineer edits only the last line so it now reads:

    enabled: true

What is the result?
choices: Process collection is enabled because comments imply the parents
The parent keys are still comments, so the setting is not nested
The Agent enables every feature whose enabled key is true
Container collection is enabled instead of process collection
questions.explanation: Commented lines do not exist as far as the YAML parser is concerned, so enabled: true is not inside process_config and process_collection; it becomes a stray key or causes a parse error. The example file says to uncomment the parameter and the one below it; uncommenting every level while keeping the indentation puts the value at process_config.process_collection.enabled.

questions.question: A tool accepts only standard JSON. Which element would make the file invalid?
choices: A comment line beginning with //
An array of objects nested in an object
The value null used for an empty field
A number written without quotes
questions.explanation: The JSON grammar defines objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false and null and has no comment syntax, so // or # comment lines make a document invalid. Nesting arrays and objects is allowed, null is a valid value, and numbers are written without quotes.

choices: enabled is a boolean and port is a number
Both values are strings
enabled is a boolean and port is a string
enabled is a string and port is a number
questions.explanation: In JSON, anything wrapped in double quotes is a string, so "true" is a four-character string rather than the boolean, which would be written true without quotes. 8126 has no quotes, so it is a number. A tool that expects a boolean may reject or misread the quoted value.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid JSON document?
choices: {"env": "prod", "port": 8080,}
{'env': 'prod', 'port': 8080}
{"env": "prod", "port": 8080}
{env: "prod", port: 8080}
questions.explanation: JSON names and string values must be wrapped in double quotes, and the grammar has no trailing comma after the last name/value pair. Single-quoted strings and unquoted keys are accepted by JavaScript and some lenient parsers, but they are not valid JSON.

questions.question:
Datadog's custom check guide uses this conf.d/custom_checkvalue.yaml:

init_config:
instances:
  [{}]

What does instances contain?
choices: No instances, so the check never runs
One instance with no instance-level settings
An empty string, which the Agent ignores
A syntax error, because [ ] is not valid YAML
questions.explanation: [{}] is YAML flow syntax for a list (square brackets) holding one empty mapping (curly braces), so the Agent schedules exactly one instance of the check with no instance-level options. Flow collections are valid YAML, and an empty list would be written [] instead. init_config: with nothing after it is simply an empty (null) value.

questions.question:
An engineer adds this line to datadog.yaml:

site:datadoghq.eu

Why does it not set the Agent's site?
choices: A mapping needs a space after the colon
The value must be wrapped in double quotes
Keys must be written in uppercase
The line must start with a dash
questions.explanation: YAML separates a key from its value with a colon followed by whitespace (key: value). Without the space, site:datadoghq.eu is read as one plain string instead of the key site, so the setting is not applied, and in a full file it can break parsing. Quoting the value is optional, datadog.yaml keys are lowercase, and a dash would turn the line into a list entry.

questions.question: In YAML, which block scalar indicator keeps every line break of a multi-line string exactly as written?
choices: > (folded)
| (literal)
- (sequence entry)
& (anchor)
questions.explanation: The literal style, introduced with |, preserves line breaks exactly. The folded style (>) turns single line breaks into spaces, while - starts a sequence entry and & defines an anchor; neither of those creates a multi-line string.

questions.question:
A custom check reads a version string from its instance:

instances:
  - app_version: 1.10

The check receives 1.1 instead of 1.10. What fixes it?
choices: Indent app_version with a tab
Add a trailing zero: app_version: 1.100
Quote the value: app_version: "1.10"
Move app_version under init_config
questions.explanation: An unquoted 1.10 matches YAML's number format, so it is loaded as the float 1.1 and the trailing zero is lost; quoting it forces a string. Tabs are not allowed for indentation, adding digits still produces a number, and moving the key to init_config does not change how the value is typed.

choices: Reject it, since YAML does not allow curly braces
Treat the entire line as one long string value
Parse it as a mapping, since JSON is valid YAML 1.2
Reject it, since YAML keys must never be quoted
questions.explanation: YAML 1.2 was designed as a superset of JSON, so a JSON object is valid YAML flow syntax and yields the same init_config and instances structure. YAML itself uses {} for flow mappings and [] for flow sequences, and quoted keys are allowed. Block style is still preferred because it is easier to read and comment.

questions.question:
This logs section of a conf.yaml fails to load:

logs:
  - type: file
    path: /var/log/app.log
     service: app
    source: python

What is the error?
choices: service is not aligned with its sibling keys
Values with slashes, like the path, must be quoted
Every key in the entry needs its own dash
The key must be log, not logs, in conf.yaml
questions.explanation: Keys in the same mapping must start in the same column. Because service is one space deeper than path, the parser treats it as a continuation of the path value and fails with a mapping error. Unquoted paths with slashes are fine, a dash starts a new list entry rather than marking each key, and logs is the documented key name.

questions.question: In an integration's conf.yaml.example, why do most parameters appear with a leading #?
choices: The # marks parameters that are deprecated
Optional parameters are commented out by default
The # marks values the Agent fills in at startup
Required parameters are commented out by default
questions.explanation: Datadog's configuration file conventions state that all optional parameters are commented by default, while required parameters are not commented. You enable an option by removing the # and setting a value. The Agent does not fill in commented values, and # has no special deprecation meaning.

questions.question: Every Datadog Agent check class must implement one entry-point method. Which one?
choices: run(self, config)
check(self, instance)
collect(self)
main(instance, init_config)
questions.explanation: Agent checks subclass AgentCheck and must implement check(self, instance); the Agent calls it on each run and passes the configuration of one entry from the instances list. The other names are not the documented entry point, and a check does not receive the whole YAML file or only init_config.

choices: The gauge is sent once, when the class is defined
The check runs but reports custom.disk.free as 0
Python raises an IndentationError and the check fails to load
Python ignores the indentation and runs it normally
questions.explanation: In Python, indentation defines blocks, and the body of a function must be indented deeper than its def line. Here self.gauge(...) sits at the same level as def check, so the function has no body and Python raises an IndentationError, which stops the check from loading. Python never ignores indentation, and no metric is sent.

questions.question:
A custom check's instance is configured as:

instances:
  - url: http://localhost:8080

Its check method starts with:

url = instance.get('url')
timeout = instance['timeout']

What happens on the second line?
choices: A KeyError is raised; timeout is missing
timeout is set to None, just like with get()
timeout is set to the default of 15 seconds
timeout is set to the url value instead
questions.explanation: The instance is a Python dict. Indexing with instance['timeout'] raises KeyError when the key is missing, whereas instance.get('timeout') would return None, or a default you pass such as instance.get('timeout', 5). Nothing fills in 15 seconds; that is the default check collection interval, not a dictionary value.

questions.question:
This line appears in Datadog's custom check example:

self.gauge('hello.world', 1, tags=['TAG_KEY:TAG_VALUE'] + self.instance.get('tags', []))

If the instance has no tags key, which tags does the gauge get?
choices: No tags, because get() returns None
Just the one tag, 'TAG_KEY:TAG_VALUE'
The call fails with a KeyError
'TAG_KEY:TAG_VALUE' plus an empty tag
questions.explanation: get('tags', []) returns the default empty list when the key is missing, and adding an empty list to a list leaves it unchanged, so only TAG_KEY:TAG_VALUE is sent. get() with a default never raises KeyError, and concatenating [] adds no elements rather than an empty tag.

questions.question: Inside an AgentCheck, which method reports whether a service is up by sending a status such as self.OK, self.WARNING or self.CRITICAL?
choices: self.gauge()
self.event()
self.service_check()
self.monotonic_count()
questions.explanation: service_check(name, status, ...) submits a service check with a status constant such as OK, WARNING or CRITICAL, as in Datadog's example integration. gauge() and monotonic_count() submit metric values, and event() submits an event rather than an up/down status.

questions.question: A Python service is normally started with python app.py. How do you add ddtrace automatic instrumentation without changing its code?
choices: python app.py --ddtrace
DD_TRACE_ENABLED=true python app.py
pip install ddtrace, then python app.py
ddtrace-run python app.py
questions.explanation: After installing ddtrace with pip, Datadog's docs instrument a Python app by prefixing its entry-point command with ddtrace-run. Installing the package alone patches nothing, --ddtrace is just an argument passed to the app, and DD_TRACE_ENABLED (default true) only controls whether trace data is sent once a tracer is loaded.

questions.question: The checkout service's code does not import ddtrace. Which command starts it so its traces carry env:staging, service:checkout and version:2.1?
choices: DD_ENV=staging DD_SERVICE=checkout DD_VERSION=2.1 ddtrace-run python app.py
DD_ENV=staging DD_SERVICE=checkout DD_VERSION=2.1 python app.py
DD_TRACE_ENV=staging DD_TRACE_SERVICE=checkout DD_TRACE_VERSION=2.1 ddtrace-run python app.py
ddtrace-run python app.py --env staging --service checkout --version 2.1
questions.explanation: ddtrace reads the unified service tagging variables DD_ENV, DD_SERVICE and DD_VERSION, and ddtrace-run loads the tracer for code that does not import it. Without ddtrace-run (or import ddtrace.auto) nothing is instrumented, the DD_TRACE_-prefixed names are not the documented variables, and flags after app.py go to the application, not the tracer.

questions.question: A Django app runs under ddtrace-run. The team wants to keep all other tracing but stop the Django integration from being patched. Which setting does this?
choices: DD_TRACE_ENABLED=false
DD_DJANGO_DISTRIBUTED_TRACING=false
DD_TRACE_DJANGO_ENABLED=false
DD_TRACE_DEBUG=false
questions.explanation: DD_TRACE_<INTEGRATION>_ENABLED toggles whether one integration is patched, and the ddtrace docs use DD_TRACE_DJANGO_ENABLED=false as the example. DD_TRACE_ENABLED=false stops sending all trace data, DD_DJANGO_DISTRIBUTED_TRACING only controls distributed tracing for that integration, and DD_TRACE_DEBUG controls tracer debug logging.

questions.question: A developer sets the service name in code through ddtrace's config API and exports DD_ENV=prod. Running ddtrace-run --info shows env prod but not the new service name. Why?
choices: --info prints only the ddtrace version and install path
ddtrace ignores any service name that is set in code
--info shows env var settings, not changes made in code
DD_ENV takes precedence and hides all other settings
questions.explanation: ddtrace-run --info prints a tracer health check and configuration, but the docs note it does not reflect configuration changes made at the code level, only environment variable configuration. The code-level service name still applies when the app runs; the Service Config view in Datadog shows the runtime configuration.

questions.question:
On a host with the default datadog.yaml, an admin runs:

grep -q "logs_enabled: true" /etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml
echo $?

No line matches. What is printed?
choices: 0, because grep itself ran without crashing
The number of matching lines, which is 0
1, the non-zero status grep uses when nothing matches
Nothing, because -q suppresses all output
questions.explanation: $? expands to the exit status of the most recently executed command, and grep exits 0 when a line is selected and 1 when none is. -q only silences grep's own output, so echo still prints the status. Exit statuses signal success or failure; they are not match counts.

questions.question:
A deploy script runs:

./validate_config.sh && sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent

validate_config.sh exits with status 1. What happens?
choices: The restart is skipped and the list returns 1
The restart runs, then the list returns 1
The restart runs because && ignores failures
The shell retries the validation script
questions.explanation: In an AND list (cmd1 && cmd2), cmd2 runs only if cmd1 returns an exit status of zero. Because the validation returned 1, the restart never runs and the list's status is 1. To run a command only when the first one fails you would use ||, and the shell never retries commands on its own.

questions.question:
In a fresh shell where DD_SITE was never set, an admin installs the Agent with:

DD_API_KEY=abc123 DD_SITE="datadoghq.eu" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"

Afterwards they run echo $DD_SITE in the same shell. What is printed?
choices: datadoghq.eu
An empty line
datadoghq.com
An error: DD_SITE is read-only
questions.explanation: Assignments placed before a command become part of that command's environment only while it runs; they are not set or exported in the calling shell. The install script sees DD_SITE, but the interactive shell does not, so echo prints an empty line. To keep the value for later commands you would run export DD_SITE=datadoghq.eu.

questions.question:
In the Agent install one-liner

DD_API_KEY=<KEY> DD_SITE="datadoghq.com" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"

what does the "$(curl -L ...)" part do?
choices: Saves the script to disk under a name taken from the URL
Tests that the URL is reachable and passes 0 or 1 to bash
Downloads the script and passes its text to bash -c to execute
Posts DD_API_KEY to the URL to register the host first
questions.explanation: $(command) is command substitution: curl's output (the script body) replaces the expression, and bash -c reads and executes that string as commands. curl writes to standard output here instead of saving a file, substitution passes output rather than an exit status, and the API key reaches the script as an environment variable, not through curl.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of tags in Datadog?
choices: Encrypt telemetry before the Agent sends it
Add dimensions for filtering and grouping data
Set the retention period for each metric in Datadog
Pick which Datadog site receives the data
questions.explanation: Datadog describes tags as a way of adding dimensions to telemetry so it can be filtered, aggregated and compared, for example viewing CPU across every host that runs one service. Tags do not encrypt data, control retention, or select the Datadog site.

questions.question: A tag can be written as prod or as env:prod. Why does Datadog recommend the env:prod form?
choices: It supports richer queries, like grouping by key
Value-only tags are dropped when data is ingested
Only key:value tags count toward the 200-character limit
Value-only tags are converted into host names
questions.explanation: Both formats are accepted, but Datadog recommends <key>:<value> because it is semantically clearer and allows richer querying, such as grouping by the key. Value-only tags are not dropped or turned into host names, and the 200-character limit applies to the whole tag string in either format.

questions.question: An EC2 instance has the AWS tag costcenter:42, and the AWS integration is set up. Logs shipped by the Agent on that instance arrive with costcenter:42 even though no log configuration mentions it. Why?
choices: The log pipeline parsed the tag out of each log message
The Agent adds every AWS tag in the account to all logs
Data from a host inherits that host's host-level tags at ingestion
Logs always receive every tag defined in the organization
questions.explanation: During ingestion, metrics, logs and traces go through host-tag inheritance: because the data is associated with a hostname, it inherits that host's host-level tags, which can come from the cloud provider or the Agent. For logs, the reserved host attribute is what lets Datadog find the matching host. The tag is not parsed from the message, and only that host's tags are applied.

questions.question: A host is tagged service:my-host, and a pod running on it is tagged service:my-service. What happens to the pod's telemetry, and what does Datadog recommend?
choices: The pod value overrides the host value; no change is needed
The host value overrides the pod value; remove the pod tag
It gets both; use a distinct host key like infra_service
Datadog rejects data carrying two service tags
questions.explanation: Because tags are inherited from multiple sources, the pod's data inherits both service:my-host and service:my-service. Datadog recommends unique, specific key names, such as infra_service for the host-level tag, to avoid duplicate keys. Neither value overrides the other, and the data is not rejected.

questions.question: Which reserved log attribute does Datadog use to correlate a log with the trace that produced it?
choices: service
trace_id
message
sourcecategory
questions.explanation: The reserved trace_id attribute holds the trace ID and is used to link a log to its trace. service names the application and lets you pivot between logs and APM, message holds the log body, and sourcecategory is an optional log configuration field rather than a reserved attribute.

questions.question: An application's logs arrive with service:web-store, but its APM traces report service:webstore. What does this mismatch mainly affect?
choices: Pivoting between the service's logs and its APM traces
Whether the logs get parsed by the right pipeline
Whether log timestamps are shown in UTC
How long the logs are retained in their index
questions.explanation: The reserved service attribute is used to switch from Logs to APM, so Datadog asks you to use the same value in both products; unified service tagging applies the same idea across all telemetry. Integration parsers are matched on source, and timestamps and retention are not tied to the service name.

questions.question: You add a log facet manually from the Log Explorer facet list. How do you reference the tag team versus the JSON attribute http.status_code?
choices: @team for the tag and http.status_code for the attribute
team for the tag and @http.status_code for the attribute
#team for the tag and $http.status_code for the attribute
tag:team and attr:http.status_code, with explicit prefixes
questions.explanation: When defining a facet, Datadog says to use the tag key name for tags and the attribute path with an @ prefix for attributes. Search follows the same convention: @ marks an attribute search, while tags are queried by key directly. The #, $, tag: and attr: prefixes are not used.

choices: All three fields are converted into tags on the log event
Body from message, level from status, amount as attribute
message is dropped, status is a tag, amount a metric
amount becomes the log body and the rest are dropped
questions.explanation: Datadog ingests the reserved message attribute as the log body used for full-text search and the reserved status attribute as the log's level. Other JSON keys such as amount are kept as attributes that you can search with @amount or turn into a facet or measure. JSON fields are not automatically turned into tags or metrics.

questions.question: Where in Datadog do you look up a host's operating system, cloud provider, tags and the Agent integrations enabled on it?
choices: The Metrics Summary page
The Infrastructure (Host) List
The Log Explorer facet panel
The Monitor Status page
questions.explanation: The Host List (Infrastructure > Hosts, also called the Infrastructure List) is a live inventory of hosts: its Configurations column shows cloud provider, OS and Agent status, the Integrations column lists enabled Agent integrations, and the host panel shows tags, metrics and Agent configuration. Metrics Summary describes metrics, the Log Explorer searches logs, and monitor pages show alert state.

questions.question: Which reserved tag key does Datadog list for assigning ownership of resources?
choices: team
env
service
device
questions.explanation: Datadog's table of reserved tag keys lists team for assigning ownership to any resource. service scopes application data across metrics, traces and logs, device segregates data by device or disk, and env scopes data by environment.

questions.question: Different teams log the client IP as clientIP, client_ip_address and remote_address. What does Datadog recommend so everyone can search one field?
choices: Create one facet per variant and search all three
Convert each variant into a host tag on ingestion
Rename the fields in every application's source code
Alias the variants to one standard attribute such as network.client.ip
questions.explanation: Datadog's naming convention uses standard attributes (such as network.client.ip) as its backbone, and aliasing maps non-standard source attributes onto a standard one without changing each team's technical stack. Separate facets keep the data fragmented, host tags are the wrong kind of metadata, and rewriting every application is what aliasing avoids.

questions.question: Which three telemetry types are commonly called the three pillars of observability?
choices: Dashboards, monitors and notebooks
Metrics, logs and traces
Hosts, containers and functions
Events, alerts and incidents
questions.explanation: Metrics (numeric measurements over time), logs (chronological records of events) and traces (the path of a request through a system) are the three pillars. Dashboards, monitors and notebooks are ways to view or act on that data, hosts and containers are what you monitor, and alerts and incidents are outcomes.

questions.question: A checkout request is slow and passes through five microservices. Which telemetry type best shows how much time each service call added?
choices: Host metrics
Log messages
Distributed traces
Synthetic test results
questions.explanation: A distributed trace records one request's flow from the frontend through each backend component, with a timed span for each operation, so it shows where latency builds up. Host metrics show resource usage, logs record discrete events, and Synthetic tests time simulated requests end to end rather than each service in the real request.

questions.question: A capacity planner wants a 30-day trend of memory usage across a cluster to forecast when to add nodes. Which telemetry type fits best?
choices: Metrics
Logs
Traces
Session replays
questions.explanation: Metrics are quantitative measurements of performance and resource utilization over time, which makes them the basis for trend analysis and forecasting. Logs and traces describe individual events and requests, and session replays show individual user sessions in RUM.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts monitoring with observability?
choices: Monitoring covers only metrics; observability covers only logs
Monitoring asks if it works; observability asks why it behaves so
Monitoring is for cloud hosts; observability is for on-prem hosts
Monitoring needs an Agent; observability works without collecting data
questions.explanation: Monitoring answers 'Is the system working?' with predefined checks and dashboards, while observability uses rich, queryable telemetry to answer 'Why is the system behaving this way?', including for problems nobody anticipated. The difference is not about a single data type or hosting model, and observability still depends on collecting telemetry.

questions.question: Which Datadog product simulates requests and user journeys from locations around the world, so you can test an app or API even when no real users are active?
choices: Real User Monitoring
Synthetic Monitoring
APM
Cloud Network Monitoring
questions.explanation: Synthetic Monitoring runs API, multistep API, browser and mobile tests from managed or private locations, on a schedule, on demand or from CI/CD pipelines. RUM measures what real users experience, APM traces requests handled by your code, and Cloud Network Monitoring analyzes network flows.

questions.question: A team wants to see traffic volume and dependencies between services, containers and availability zones, built from connection data at the IP, port and PID level. Which product fits?
choices: Application Performance Monitoring (APM)
Synthetic Monitoring (Synthetics)
Cloud Network Monitoring (formerly NPM)
Real User Monitoring (RUM)
questions.explanation: Cloud Network Monitoring (formerly Network Performance Monitoring) aggregates IP-, port- and PID-level connection data into dependencies between endpoints and shows them on a network page and network map. APM traces application requests, Synthetic Monitoring runs simulated tests, and RUM measures real users' browser and mobile sessions.

questions.question: Which Datadog security product is powered by Log Management and detects real-time threats such as an IP address that matches a threat-intelligence list?
choices: Cloud SIEM
Code Security
Sensitive Data Scanner
Synthetic Monitoring
questions.explanation: Cloud SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) analyzes ingested logs to detect threats such as targeted attacks or communication with IPs on threat-intel lists. Code Security scans code and open source libraries for vulnerabilities, Sensitive Data Scanner finds sensitive data such as PII, and Synthetic Monitoring tests availability and performance.

questions.question: Your team logs in to Datadog at https://ap1.datadoghq.com. Which value belongs in the Agent's site setting?
choices: datadoghq.com
app.ap1.datadoghq.com
ap1.datadoghq.com
datadoghq.jp
questions.explanation: Datadog's site table maps the AP1 site URL https://ap1.datadoghq.com to the site parameter ap1.datadoghq.com, located in Japan. datadoghq.com is US1, which the Agent uses when site is not set, and the other values are not site parameters.

questions.question: A company has one Datadog organization on US1 and another on EU1. Can a US1 dashboard display data stored in the EU1 organization?
choices: Yes, once both organizations are linked as multi-org
No, each site is independent and data cannot be shared
Yes, if the dashboard's time zone is set to CET
Yes, but only for metrics and not for logs
questions.explanation: Datadog's sites documentation states that each site is completely independent and you cannot share data across sites. To see the same data in both, you would have to send it to both destinations (see the Dual Shipping guide). Organization linking, time zones and data type do not change this.

questions.question: A German company requires that its monitoring data be stored in the EU. Which Datadog site should it use?
choices: US1 (datadoghq.com)
EU1 (datadoghq.eu)
US5 (us5.datadoghq.com)
AP1 (ap1.datadoghq.com)
questions.explanation: Datadog sites let you store data in specific locations; EU1 (site parameter datadoghq.eu, app at https://app.datadoghq.eu) is located in Germany. US1 and US5 are located in the US, and AP1 is located in Japan.

questions.question: A US government agency needs Datadog's FedRAMP High certified site. Which site does it use?
choices: US1-FED (ddog-gov.com)
US3 (us3.datadoghq.com)
US5 (us5.datadoghq.com)
US1 (datadoghq.com)
questions.explanation: The Datadog for Government site US1-FED (site parameter ddog-gov.com, app at https://app.ddog-gov.com) is Datadog's FedRAMP High certified site, meant for US government agencies and partners. US1, US3 and US5 are commercial sites located in the US.

questions.question: An organization's Datadog account is on US3. An admin installs the Agent, sets only api_key in datadog.yaml, and leaves # site: "datadoghq.com" commented out. No data appears in the US3 account. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Agent needs an application key to send data
The Agent sends to the default US1 site, not US3
US3 accepts data only through the API, not the Agent
The site line must stay commented out for US3
questions.explanation: The datadog.yaml example documents site as optional with a default of datadoghq.com (US1). With it commented out, the Agent reports to US1, and because sites are independent the US3 organization never sees the data; setting site: us3.datadoghq.com fixes it. The Agent needs an API key and the correct site, not an application key, and US3 accepts Agent data like any other site.

questions.question: Why does the Datadog documentation include a site selector dropdown?
choices: It translates the docs into the site's local language
Features, endpoints and settings can vary by Datadog site
It moves your organization's data to the chosen site
It picks the nearest docs mirror for faster loading
questions.explanation: Different Datadog sites may support different functionality depending on each instance's security requirements, so the docs show site-specific details, such as endpoints and government-site differences, for the selected site. Language is chosen separately, and the selector never moves data because sites are independent.

questions.question: Datadog is delivered as SaaS. Which statement describes how data from an Agent reaches the platform?
choices: Datadog connects in to each host to pull its data
You host Datadog's backend database on your own servers
The Agent initiates outbound encrypted connections
The Agent serves dashboards locally on each host
questions.explanation: Datadog runs the platform for you; the Agent collects data locally and sends it to Datadog. The network docs state that traffic is always initiated by the Agent, no sessions are ever initiated from Datadog back to the Agent, and all Agent traffic is sent over SSL. You do not host the backend, and dashboards are served by the Datadog web app.

questions.question: Which pairing of a Datadog building block and its purpose is correct?
choices: Monitor: alerts the team when critical changes occur
Dashboard: collects metrics from the host's processes
Integration: defines the alert thresholds for metrics
Agent: renders graphs for users in the web browser
questions.explanation: Datadog's Getting Started describes monitors as alerts and notifications that tell your team when critical changes occur. The Agent is software on your hosts that sends metrics and events to Datadog, integrations layer Datadog over technologies you already use (alert thresholds are set in monitors), and dashboards visualize data rather than collect it.

questions.question: What does Datadog's Logging without Limits approach let a team do?
choices: Store every log in an index forever at no extra cost
Ingest and process all logs, then pick what to index
Send logs to Datadog without installing any collector
Skip parsing, since logs are indexed as raw text only
questions.explanation: Logging without Limits decouples log ingestion from indexing, so you can collect, process, archive and monitor all logs while choosing which ones to index, for example with exclusion filters. It does not make indexing unlimited or free, it still relies on log collection, and pipelines still parse logs.

questions.question: In a monitoring context, what does metadata usually refer to?
choices: Information about the data, such as hostnames, tags, and cloud attributes
Only raw CPU percentages
Encrypted secrets stored in the Agent
Dashboard screenshots
questions.explanation: Metadata is descriptive context attached to telemetry, such as host identity, region, team, or environment. Datadog uses that context to filter, group, correlate, and navigate between related signals.

questions.question: What is Datadog's Service Catalog primarily used for?
choices: Compiling Agent integration packages locally
Rotating API keys for services
Storing raw log archives for compliance
Discovering, inventorying, and managing metadata and ownership for services in your estate
questions.explanation: Service Catalog aggregates services observed across metrics, traces, logs, and real-user monitoring into a single inventory. Teams use it to attach ownership, tier, on-call, and metadata so service health and dependencies are easier to navigate.

questions.question: What is Bits (AI) Chat in Datadog used for?
choices: Generating Kubernetes pod annotations automatically
Encrypting API keys before they are stored
Asking natural-language questions to investigate data and run triage across telemetry
Compiling custom Agent binaries
questions.explanation: Bits (AI) Chat is Datadog's assistant for interacting with telemetry in natural language. It can help query data, summarize investigations, and suggest next steps across dashboards, logs, metrics, and incidents.

questions.question: An engineer edits datadog.yaml with a tab character for indentation. Why can this break the Agent configuration?
choices: The Agent requires UTF-16 text files
YAML indentation is whitespace-sensitive, and tabs commonly invalidate parsing
Tabs automatically expose the API key in plaintext
Tabs force the Agent to switch from TCP to UDP
questions.explanation: YAML parsers rely on clean, consistent indentation to understand nested structure. Tabs are a common source of syntax errors, which can prevent the Agent from loading the configuration at all.

questions.question: Which format is commonly used for Datadog Agent configuration because it is human-readable and supports nested key-value data?
choices: CSV
Plain text without structure
YAML
Markdown
questions.explanation: The Datadog Agent's main configuration file is `datadog.yaml`, which uses YAML syntax. YAML is easy for humans to read and is well suited to nested settings such as lists of tags and integration options.

questions.question: In a YAML configuration file such as datadog.yaml, what do leading spaces usually control?
choices: Network bandwidth
Structure and nesting
TLS encryption
File ownership
questions.explanation: YAML uses indentation to show which settings belong under other settings. If the nesting is wrong, the Agent may read a value under the wrong parent key or fail to parse the file.

questions.question: Which Datadog product analyzes network traffic between services, hosts, containers, and availability zones to help identify dependencies and bottlenecks?
choices: Metrics Explorer
Network Performance Monitoring
Host Map
Service Catalog
questions.explanation: Network Performance Monitoring (NPM) collects and correlates network-level traffic data so teams can visualize dependencies, find noisy neighbors, and troubleshoot connectivity or latency between services and endpoints across cloud and on-prem environments.

questions.question: In Datadog Infrastructure & Cloud Network Monitoring, what does a connection between two endpoints in the network map typically represent?
choices: A dashboard template variable
A static firewall rule exported from a router
A pending Agent installation
Observed network traffic or a dependency between two services, hosts, or containers over a selected time window
questions.explanation: The network map in Datadog's Infrastructure & Cloud Network Monitoring visualizes observed traffic and dependencies between endpoints. Edges reflect actual flow data over the selected window, which makes service dependencies and bottlenecks easier to spot than with static topology diagrams.

questions.question: A team needs automation with loops, conditionals, and API calls around Datadog tasks. What is the role of a programming language such as Python in that workflow?
choices: It removes the need to know shell commands
It changes the Agent into a kernel module
It auto-discovers containers without configuration
It can execute automation logic and call Datadog tools or APIs programmatically
questions.explanation: A programming language gives you a way to express automation logic in code, including API calls and conditional behavior. Datadog is still the target system; the language is simply the tool used to automate around it.

questions.question: Which example shows a valid YAML list of tags for a Datadog config file?
choices: tags = env:prod, service:web
tags: ['env:prod', 'service:web']
tags: env:prod -> service:web
tags: [env:prod service:web]
questions.explanation: YAML accepts list syntax in brackets when the items are comma separated. That represents two distinct tag strings, whereas the other examples are not valid YAML list syntax.

questions.question: What does the Datadog APM Service Map visualize?
choices: Hostnames sorted alphabetically
The geographic location of office buildings
API key rotation schedules
Services and the observed request-level dependencies and traffic between them
questions.explanation: The APM Service Map shows services as nodes with edges representing observed request flow and dependencies inferred from traces. It helps teams understand which services call which, and where latency, errors, or throughput concentration sit in the topology.

questions.question: What are the three pillars of observability that Datadog is built around?
choices: Dashboards, monitors, and alerts
Metrics, logs, and traces
CPU, memory, and disk
API keys, application keys, and client tokens
questions.explanation: The three pillars of observability are metrics, logs, and traces. Datadog unifies these signals so teams can correlate numerical trends, discrete event records, and request-level execution paths across the same services and environments.

questions.question: Why is indentation important in a YAML configuration file?
choices: It alphabetizes the keys
It defines the data hierarchy and nesting
It encrypts sensitive values
It controls comment color
questions.explanation: YAML uses indentation to represent structure, so the placement of spaces determines which values belong under which keys. If indentation is wrong, the Agent may read the file incorrectly or fail to load the configuration at all.

questions.question: What is an environment variable such as DD_API_KEY primarily used for when configuring the Datadog Agent?
choices: To replace the operating system's hostname permanently
To convert YAML configuration files into JSON
To encrypt all network traffic on the host automatically
To supply configuration values to a process without hardcoding them in the command itself
questions.explanation: Environment variables let software read configuration values from the process environment instead of embedding them directly in scripts or binaries. This is a common way to pass secrets and site settings to containerized or automated Agent deployments.

questions.question: An engineer adds a new setting to datadog.yaml, but the Agent fails to start because of a YAML error. Which mistake is most likely?
choices: Using tabs or inconsistent indentation in the YAML structure
Adding comments that start with #
Writing keys in lowercase letters
Using consistent indentation for nested keys
questions.explanation: YAML is whitespace-sensitive, so indentation must be consistent for nested structures to parse correctly. Tabs and mismatched indentation commonly break configuration files such as datadog.yaml.

questions.question: In Datadog APM, what is a trace?
choices: A single numeric metric sample collected at a timestamp
A line of text emitted from a log file
A request-level execution path made up of spans that show how a request moves through services
A snapshot of host CPU and memory usage
questions.explanation: A trace represents the journey of a single request through one or more services. It is composed of spans, each capturing a unit of work with timing, tags, and resource metadata so teams can see where latency or errors originate across distributed services.

questions.question: Why must indentation be consistent in `datadog.yaml`?
choices: Because `DD_SITE` must appear in the first column
Because Datadog sorts YAML keys by whitespace depth before sending
Because YAML uses whitespace indentation to represent nesting and structure
Because the Agent only accepts tab characters in YAML
questions.explanation: YAML uses indentation to express hierarchy. Incorrect spacing can move a setting into the wrong scope or make the configuration invalid.

questions.question: What best describes an environment variable such as `DD_API_KEY` when used to configure the Agent?
choices: A dashboard variable generated by the Datadog UI
A runtime value the operating system provides to the Agent process
A host tag automatically inherited by every metric
A secret stored only in Datadog cloud
questions.explanation: Environment variables are values the operating system or process launcher passes to a running program. The Datadog Agent can read many `DD_` variables as alternatives to file-based settings.

questions.question: In observability, what is metadata?
choices: An encrypted archive of logs
A compiled Agent binary
Descriptive context such as hostnames, tags, and cloud attributes
The numeric value of a metric sample
questions.explanation: Metadata adds context around telemetry so you can filter, group, and understand what a data point represents. Examples include host names, instance types, regions, and tags like env:prod.

questions.question: Which data format is commonly used for Datadog APIs and many other web service request bodies?
choices: Bash aliases
ELF
JSON
INI comments
questions.explanation: JSON is a structured text format based on key-value pairs and arrays, which makes it well suited for APIs. Datadog's public APIs commonly accept and return JSON payloads.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts logs and metrics as observability signals?
choices: Metrics are numeric timeseries that capture trends, while logs are discrete records that capture what happened at a moment
Logs and metrics are the same signal stored in different places
Metrics can only come from logs after parsing
Logs are timestamped numeric points, while metrics are discrete event records
questions.explanation: Metrics are numeric timeseries well suited to tracking rates, utilization, and trends over time. Logs are discrete records of events or transactions that add detail such as request bodies, stack traces, or messages. Datadog correlates both so context from each can be used together.

questions.question: A service's metadata in Service Catalog is missing an on-call team. What is the most practical way to keep that metadata current as ownership changes?
choices: Email the change to Datadog Support each quarter
Define service definitions through the Service Catalog API or integrations so ownership is stored as code and updated alongside deployments
Edit the host's /etc/hostname file
Rotate the API key every time ownership changes
questions.explanation: Service Catalog metadata such as on-call, tier, and ownership can be defined through the Service Catalog API, Terraform, or integrations with tools like PagerDuty and ServiceNow. Storing definitions as code keeps metadata current without manual UI edits each time ownership changes.

questions.question: In Datadog, what does host or cloud metadata mainly provide?
choices: A replacement for all monitor thresholds
A compression method for metric payloads
A required license file for the Agent
Context such as cloud attributes, host details, and labels that enrich telemetry
questions.explanation: Metadata adds context like cloud region, instance type, container labels, or host details. That context makes filtering, grouping, and attribution more useful once the data is in Datadog.

questions.question: Which of the following is metadata rather than a timeseries metric?
choices: system.cpu.user
system.mem.used
os:linux
system.disk.in_use
questions.explanation: A tag like os:linux is descriptive metadata that helps with filtering and grouping. Metrics such as CPU, memory, and disk utilization are numerical timeseries values that change over time.

questions.question: Which metadata tag would be most useful for grouping all database servers in Datadog?
choices: uptime:10432
region:us-east-1
role:database
kernel:5.15
questions.explanation: A tag like role:database expresses what the host does, which makes it useful for scoping dashboards, monitors, and investigations. The other values may still be informative, but they do not directly identify database servers as a functional group.

questions.question: A team wants to automate dashboard creation through the Datadog API. Which tool is the most appropriate starting point?
choices: A spreadsheet that has no HTTP support
An image editor
A Python script that makes HTTP requests to the Datadog API
A BIOS setup utility
questions.explanation: The Datadog API is an HTTP REST API, so a scripting language with HTTP support is a practical way to automate it. Python is a common choice because it can easily handle authentication, JSON payloads, and repeatable workflows.

questions.question: A tag value in `datadog.yaml` contains a colon and spaces. Why might quoting that value be safer in YAML?
choices: It makes the tag case-insensitive across Datadog
It helps YAML avoid misreading special characters as structure
It forces the Agent to encrypt the value before upload
It converts the value into a monitor variable
questions.explanation: Quoting is useful when values contain colons, hashes, or other characters YAML might interpret specially. It helps preserve the exact literal string you intended to set.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts YAML and JSON in common Datadog workflows?
choices: YAML is only for dashboards, while JSON is only for shell scripts
YAML is often used for Agent configuration, while Datadog API responses commonly use JSON
YAML cannot store strings
JSON cannot represent arrays
questions.explanation: Datadog Agent configuration files are commonly written in YAML, while Datadog's REST API uses JSON for request and response bodies. Both formats can represent structured data, but they are used in different parts of typical Datadog workflows.

questions.question: An engineer edits a YAML file and replaces the indentation spaces with tabs. What is the most likely result?
choices: Datadog automatically converts the tabs to spaces
The file becomes valid JSON
Only the comments are affected
The YAML parser may reject the file
questions.explanation: YAML is sensitive to indentation rules, and tabs commonly cause parsing problems. In practice, that can prevent the Agent from loading the changed configuration and delay data collection until the formatting is fixed.

flashcards.back:
key: value pairs (a space after the colon)
Indent nested maps with spaces, never tabs
List items start with '- '
# starts a comment
Sibling keys must share the same indentation

flashcards.front: Two equivalent ways to write a YAML list
flashcards.back:
Block style:
tags:
  - env:prod
  - team:web
Flow style:
tags: ["env:prod", "team:web"]
Datadog treats both as the same list.

| (literal) keeps every line break exactly as written.
> (folded) joins lines with spaces (blank lines still become line breaks).

flashcards.front: When should you quote a YAML value?
flashcards.back: When it contains ': ' or ' #', starts with a special character such as *, &, !, [ or {, or looks like a number or boolean that must stay a string (for example "1.10" or "true").

flashcards.front: Does # always start a comment in YAML?
flashcards.back: No. # starts a comment only when it is separated from other tokens by whitespace, so in url: http://host/page#top the #top stays part of the value.

Objects {"key": value}, arrays [a, b]
Keys and strings use double quotes
Values: string, number, true, false, null, object, array
No comments, no trailing commas
YAML 1.2 is a superset of JSON, so valid JSON is valid YAML. YAML uses indentation, allows # comments and unquoted strings; JSON uses braces and brackets, requires double quotes and has no comments.

flashcards.front: How are Datadog's example config files (datadog.yaml, conf.yaml.example) laid out?
flashcards.back: Required parameters are uncommented; optional parameters are commented out with #, with ## @param lines documenting them. To change one, remove the # (and uncomment any parent keys, keeping indentation), set the value, then restart the Agent.

init_config: settings applied globally to every instance
instances: a list; each '- ' entry is one instance the check runs against
logs: (optional) log collection entries

flashcards.front: Reading a check: what do class X(AgentCheck), def check(self, instance) and self.gauge(name, value) mean?
flashcards.back:
class X(AgentCheck): X inherits from Datadog's AgentCheck base class.
def check(self, instance): the method the Agent calls, with one instances entry as a dict.
self.gauge(name, value, tags=[...]): submits a gauge metric with optional tags.

Metrics: self.gauge, self.count, self.monotonic_count, self.rate, self.histogram
Status: self.service_check with OK, WARNING, CRITICAL or UNKNOWN
Events: self.event

flashcards.front: Python basics for reading check code
flashcards.back:
Indentation defines blocks (a ':' ends def/class/if/for lines); bad indentation raises IndentationError.
d['key'] raises KeyError if the key is missing; d.get('key', default) returns the default (None if omitted).
list + list concatenates.

ddtrace-run python app.py instruments supported libraries without code changes. import ddtrace.auto as the very first import does it from inside the code (not when already under ddtrace-run). ddtrace-run --info shows the environment-variable configuration.

DD_SERVICE, DD_ENV, DD_VERSION: unified service tags
DD_TRACE_ENABLED: send traces (default true)
DD_TRACE_<INTEGRATION>_ENABLED: patch one integration
DD_TRACE_DEBUG: tracer debug logs
DD_AGENT_HOST / DD_TRACE_AGENT_URL: where traces go (default http://localhost:8126)
0 = success, non-zero = failure. $? holds the status of the most recent command. 127 = command not found; 126 = found but not executable.

a | b: a's output feeds b's input (status of the last command unless pipefail)
a && b: run b only if a succeeded
a || b: run b only if a failed
a ; b: run both in sequence

flashcards.front: Anatomy of the Agent install one-liner
flashcards.back:
DD_API_KEY=<KEY> DD_SITE="<SITE>" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"
Prefix assignments set env vars for that command only; $(curl -L ...) downloads the script; bash -c runs the downloaded text.

flashcards.front: What does #!/usr/bin/env bash at the top of a script do?
flashcards.back: It is the shebang line: it tells the OS to run the script with the first bash found in $PATH. #!/bin/bash hard-codes the interpreter path instead.

flashcards.front: What is a tag in Datadog?
flashcards.back: A label that adds a dimension to telemetry so it can be filtered, aggregated and compared. Format <key>:<value> (recommended, e.g. env:prod) or <value>.

flashcards.front: Reserved tag keys and what they enable
flashcards.back:
host: correlate metrics, traces, processes, logs
device: split data by device or disk
source: span filtering, log pipelines
service, env, version: scope app data (unified service tagging)
team: ownership

Metrics, logs, traces and integrations associated with a hostname inherit that host's host-level tags (from the cloud provider or the Agent) at ingestion. Use distinct key names to avoid duplicate keys from different sources.

host, source, status, service, trace_id, message (searchable without @).
message = log body; status = level; service links to APM; trace_id links to the trace; source matches an integration to install its parsers and facets.

Attributes: key/value fields from the log content (usually JSON), searched with @ (e.g. @http.status_code); case-sensitive and not normalized.
Tags: key:value labels from the host, Agent or integration config, searched by key (e.g. env:prod).

Standard attributes (e.g. network.client.ip, http.status_code) define a naming convention. Aliasing maps non-standard attributes onto a standard one so all teams use the same facet; changes apply to newly ingested logs.

flashcards.front: What host information does the Infrastructure (Host) List show?
flashcards.back: A live inventory of hosts: hostnames and aliases, status, tags, OS, cloud provider, Agent status and configuration, detected software, enabled integrations, and metrics.

Metrics: numeric measurements over time (trends, forecasting)
Logs: timestamped records of discrete events
Traces: a request's path across services, with timed spans

Monitoring: 'Is it working?' Predefined checks, thresholds and dashboards.
Observability: 'Why is it behaving this way?' Explore rich, correlated telemetry to investigate unexpected issues.

flashcards.front: Which app URL do you log in to for each Datadog site?
flashcards.back:
US1: https://app.datadoghq.com
US3: https://us3.datadoghq.com
US5: https://us5.datadoghq.com
EU1: https://app.datadoghq.eu
AP1: https://ap1.datadoghq.com
AP2: https://ap2.datadoghq.com
UK1: https://uk1.datadoghq.com
US1-FED: https://app.ddog-gov.com
US2-FED: https://us2.ddog-gov.com

flashcards.front: Why does your Datadog site matter?
flashcards.back: Each site is completely independent (no data sharing across sites) and keeps data in a given location or meets regulations. The Agent's site / DD_SITE (default datadoghq.com), API endpoints and the docs site selector must match your organization's site.
The Datadog for Government site: FedRAMP High certified, at https://app.ddog-gov.com (site parameter ddog-gov.com), for US government agencies and partners.

flashcards.front: Core Datadog products in one line each
flashcards.back:
Infrastructure: hosts, containers, processes
APM: application traces and performance
Log Management: collect, process, search logs
RUM: real users' web/mobile experience
Synthetic Monitoring: simulated tests
Cloud Network Monitoring (formerly NPM): network flows
Security: Cloud SIEM, Cloud Security, App and API Protection

RUM measures real users' sessions (performance, errors, usage) in web and mobile apps. Synthetic Monitoring runs scripted API, browser and mobile tests from managed or private locations, even with no real traffic.

flashcards.front: Getting Started building blocks: Agent, integrations, dashboards, monitors
flashcards.back:
Agent: software on hosts that sends metrics and events
Integrations: connect the technologies you already use
Dashboards: visualize and share data
Monitors: alert when critical changes occur

flashcards.front: Integration types described in Introduction to Integrations
flashcards.back: Agent-based (installed with the Agent, Python check method), authentication/crawler-based (credentials set up in Datadog, e.g. AWS, Slack), and library integrations (language libraries using the Datadog API).

flashcards.front: What does Datadog being SaaS mean for your team?
flashcards.back: Datadog hosts and runs the platform (storage, UI, alerting) at your Datadog site; you only install the Agent and set up integrations, which send data out to Datadog. Agent connections are always outbound, over SSL.

api_key: associates the Agent's data with your organization
site: your Datadog site (default datadoghq.com), e.g. datadoghq.eu for EU1
